title: Find if Path Exists in Graph
summary: Return whether an undirected graph with n nodes has a path from source to destination.
statement:
An undirected graph has `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n − 1`; each `edges[i] = [u, v]` connects `u` and `v`. Return `true` if there is a path from `source` to `destination`.

A node always has a path to itself.
hints: This is a reachability question: do source and destination belong to the same connected component?
BFS or DFS from source over an adjacency list works in O(n + edges).
Union-find also fits: union every edge, then check find(source) == find(destination).
explain: Node 0 is joined directly to node 2 by the edge `[2,0]` (and also through 1), so a path exists and the answer is `true`.

title: Redundant Connection
summary: A tree of n nodes (labelled 1..n) had one extra edge added. Return an edge whose removal leaves a tree; if several qualify, the one that appears last in the input.
statement:
A tree with `n` nodes labelled `1` to `n` had one extra edge added, so `edges` (of length `n`) now contains exactly one cycle.

Return an edge that can be removed so the remaining edges form a tree. If several edges qualify, return the one that appears last in `edges`.
constraints: No repeated edges; the graph is connected
hints: Add the edges one by one. Which edge is the first to close a cycle?
With union-find, an edge [u, v] closes a cycle exactly when u and v already have the same root.
Because you process edges in input order, the first such edge is also the last one in the input among the cycle's edges. Return it.
explain: Edges `[1,2]` and `[1,3]` already connect all three nodes, so `[2,3]` closes a cycle. Removing it leaves a tree, and it is the last such edge, so the answer is `[2,3]`.

title: Satisfiability of Equality Equations
summary: Equations look like "a==b" or "a!=b" over single-letter variables. Return whether integers can be assigned so every equation holds.
statement:
Each string in `equations` has the form `"a==b"` or `"a!=b"`, where `a` and `b` are lowercase letters standing for integer variables.

Return `true` if you can assign integers to the variables so that every equation holds.
constraints: Each equation is four characters: a letter, "==" or "!=", and a letter
hints: Equalities group variables together; inequalities only need checking afterwards.
First pass: union the two variables of every "==" equation (26 letters, so a small union-find).
Second pass: for every "!=" equation, if both variables have the same root, the equations contradict each other. Note "a!=a" is always false.
explain: "a==b" puts a and b in the same group, but "b!=a" says they must differ. Both cannot hold, so the answer is `false`.

title: Smallest String With Swaps
summary: You may swap the characters at any listed pair of indices, any number of times. Return the lexicographically smallest string you can reach.

perf.label: a 100,000-character string with 100,000 pairs
perf.gen: String a0 = BCB.str(100000, "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"); List<List<Integer>> a1 = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 100000; i++) a1.add(Arrays.asList(BCB.rnd(0, 99999), BCB.rnd(0, 99999)));

statement:
You may swap the characters at the two indices of any pair in `pairs`, as many times as you like and in any order.

Return the lexicographically smallest string `s` can become.

Swaps chain together: if 0 can swap with 1 and 1 with 2, then the letters at 0, 1 and 2 can be arranged in any order. Group the indices, then sort the letters within each group.
hints: If index a can swap with b, and b with c, then repeated swaps can arrange the characters at a, b and c in any order.
Union the indices of every pair; each connected group of indices can be rearranged freely.
For each group, sort its characters and place them into its indices in increasing order of index.
explain: Indices 0 and 3 can swap, holding "d" and "b", so "b" goes first. Indices 1 and 2 hold "c" and "a", so "a" goes to index 1. The result is "bacd".

title: Accounts Merge
summary: Each account is [name, email…]. Accounts sharing any email belong to the same person. Return the merged accounts as [name, emails in sorted order…]; the accounts themselves may be in any order.
statement:
Each account is a list whose first element is a name and whose other elements are email addresses. Two accounts belong to the same person if they share at least one email. A person always has the same name, but different people can share a name.

Merge the accounts and return them as `[name, emails…]` with the emails sorted. The accounts themselves may be in any order.
constraints: Names and emails are 1 to 30 characters
hints: Emails are the things that link accounts. Think of each email as a node.
Union all emails within one account (for example, each with the account's first email), and remember the name for each email.
Group emails by their root, sort each group, and put the name in front.
explain: The first two John accounts share "johnsmith@mail.com", so they are the same person and merge into one account with three emails, sorted. The third John shares no email with them, so he stays separate, and Mary is on her own.

title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
summary: Connecting two points costs their Manhattan distance. Return the minimum total cost to connect every point (a minimum spanning tree).
statement:
`points[i] = [x, y]` is a point on a plane. Connecting two points costs their Manhattan distance `|x1 − x2| + |y1 − y2|`.

Return the minimum total cost to connect all points so that there is exactly one path between any two of them (a minimum spanning tree).
hints: Every pair of points is a possible edge, so the graph is complete: about n²/2 edges.
Kruskal: sort all edges by cost and add each one that joins two different components (union-find), until you have n − 1 edges.
Prim's algorithm with an O(n²) array scan, no heap needed, is ideal for a dense graph like this.
explain: Distance is |x1 − x2| + |y1 − y2|. The cheapest way to connect everything uses [0,0]–[2,2] (4), [2,2]–[5,2] (3), [5,2]–[7,0] (4) and [2,2]–[3,10] (9), for a total of 20.

title: Regions Cut By Slashes
summary: Each cell of an n×n grid holds "/", "\" or a space, cutting the cell. Return how many regions the grid is divided into.
statement:
`grid` is an `n × n` grid of 1 × 1 squares. Each square holds `'/'`, `'\'` or a space, and the slashes cut the square diagonally.

Return the number of regions the grid is divided into. (In the tests a backslash is escaped, so `"\\/"` is a backslash followed by a slash.)
constraints: Each string in grid has length n
Each character is "/", "\" or a space
hints: Split every square into 4 triangles (top, right, bottom, left) and count connected triangles.
Inside a square: a space joins all four; "/" joins top–left and right–bottom; "\" joins top–right and left–bottom.
Between squares, join a square's right triangle with the left triangle of the square to its right, and its bottom triangle with the top of the square below. Count the components with union-find.
explain: The two slashes join into one diagonal line from the bottom-left corner to the top-right corner, cutting the 2 × 2 square into 2 regions.

title: Largest Component Size by Common Factor
summary: Values are nodes; two values are connected when they share a factor greater than 1. Return the size of the largest connected component.
statement:
`nums` holds distinct positive integers. Treat each value as a node, and connect two values with an edge if they share a common factor greater than 1.

Return the number of nodes in the largest connected component.
hints: Checking every pair for a common factor is O(n²). Connect values through their factors instead.
For each value, find its prime factors (trial division up to √v) and union the value with each of them, in a union-find over 1 … max.
Two values sharing a prime end up in the same set. Count how many values have each root and return the largest count.
explain: 4 and 6 share the factor 2, 6 and 15 share 3, and 15 and 35 share 5. That chains all four numbers into one component of size 4.

title: Graph Valid Tree
summary: Nodes are labelled 0..n − 1 and edges are undirected. Return true if the edges form a valid tree: connected and without cycles.
statement:
You have a graph of `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n − 1`, and a list of undirected `edges` where `edges[i] = [a_i, b_i]`.

Return `true` if these edges make up a **valid tree**: every node is reachable from every other node, and there are no cycles.

For example `[[0,1],[1,2],[2,3],[1,3],[1,4]]` is `false`: 1, 2 and 3 form a cycle.
hints: A tree on n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges. If the count is different, you can answer straight away.
With exactly n − 1 edges, the graph is a tree if and only if it has no cycle (equivalently, if it is connected).
Union-find: for each edge, if both ends already have the same root, that edge closes a cycle. Otherwise merge their sets. DFS or BFS from node 0 that checks it reaches all n nodes also works.
explain: There are 4 edges for 5 nodes, and they connect everything without a loop: 0 joins 1, 2 and 3, and 1 joins 4. So the answer is `true`.

title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
summary: Nodes are labelled 0..n − 1 and edges are undirected. Return the number of connected components.
statement: You have a graph of `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n − 1`, and a list of undirected `edges` where `edges[i] = [a_i, b_i]`. Return the number of **connected components** in the graph: groups of nodes that can reach each other.
hints: Each DFS or BFS started from a node that has not been visited yet discovers one whole component.
Count how many times you have to start a new search.
With union-find, start with n components and subtract one every time an edge joins two different sets.
explain: Nodes 0, 1 and 2 are linked into one group, and 3 and 4 form another. That is 2 components.

title: Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges in Minimum Spanning Tree
summary: edges[i] = [a, b, weight] in a connected undirected graph. An edge is critical if every minimum spanning tree uses it, and pseudo-critical if some but not all do. Return [critical indices, pseudo-critical indices]; each list may be in any order.
statement:
You have a connected, weighted, undirected graph with `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n − 1`, and `edges[i] = [a_i, b_i, weight_i]`. A **minimum spanning tree** (MST) is a subset of edges that connects all nodes, has no cycles and has the smallest possible total weight.

- An edge is **critical** if removing it from the graph would make the MST weight larger (or the graph disconnected): every MST uses it.
- An edge is **pseudo-critical** if it appears in some MSTs but not in all of them.

Return `[critical, pseudoCritical]`: two lists of edge indices. The indices inside each list may be in any order.
hints: Compute the MST weight once with Kruskal: sort edges by weight and add each one that joins two different union-find sets.
Edge i is critical if the MST built while skipping it is heavier, or does not connect all nodes.
Otherwise, edge i is pseudo-critical if an MST built with edge i forced in first still has the optimal weight. Sort once and reuse the order: about 2E Kruskal runs in total.
explain: The MST weighs 7. Edges 0 and 1 (weight 1) are in every MST, so they are critical. Edges 2 and 3 (weight 2) are interchangeable, as are 4 and 5 (weight 3), so those four are pseudo-critical; edge 6 is in no MST. The answer is `[[0,1],[2,3,4,5]]`.

title: Greatest Common Divisor Traversal
summary: You may move between indices i and j when gcd(nums[i], nums[j]) > 1. Return true if every pair of indices is connected by some sequence of moves.
statement:
You can move between index `i` and index `j` (`i != j`) if and only if `gcd(nums[i], nums[j]) > 1`.

Return `true` if, for **every** pair of indices `i < j`, there is a sequence of moves that takes you from `i` to `j`. Otherwise return `false`.
hints: This asks whether a graph is connected. Checking the gcd of every pair builds the graph in O(n²), which is too slow for 10⁵ numbers.
Two numbers can be joined exactly when they share a prime factor. Instead of connecting numbers to numbers, connect each number to its prime factors.

Use union-find over indices plus one node per prime. Factor each value quickly with a smallest-prime-factor sieve. Watch out for 1: it has no prime factors, so it is isolated unless it is the only element.
explain: 2 and 6 share the factor 2, and 3 and 6 share the factor 3, so every index can reach every other through index 2. The answer is `true`.
